citations.quote: Let $S$ be a finite nonempty state set and let $A(s)$ be a finite nonempty action set for each $s\in S$, as in the finite-MDP convention. Put $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$ with its discrete sigma-algebra. Equip $S$ with its power-set sigma-algebra, $[0,1]$ with its Borel sigma-algebra, and $S\times[0,1]$ with the product sigma-algebra. A finite MDP with bounded real rewards specifies a probability kernel $Q$ from $D$ to $S\times[0,1]$; equivalently, each admissible $(s,a)$ has a probability measure $Q(\cdot\mid s,a)$ on that product measurable space. The reward-coordinate projection $(s',\rho)\mapsto\rho$ is measurable because the preimage of each Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$ is the product rectangle $S\times B$. Define the next-state law by $P(s'\mid s,a)=Q(\{s'\}\times[0,1]\mid s,a)$ and the mean reward by $r(s,a)=\int_{S\times[0,1]}\rho\,Q(ds',d\rho\mid s,a)\in[0,1]$. At each time, conditional on the observed history and the selected action, the next-state/reward pair has this law. Assume the Axiom of Choice for the path-space construction under policies.

Assume Choice. Let $(E_n,\mathcal E_n)_{n\ge0}$ be measurable spaces, let
$\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $E_0$, and, for each $n\ge0$, let $K_n$ be
a probability kernel from $E_0\times\cdots\times E_n$ to $E_{n+1}$. There is a
unique probability measure $P$ on
$$ \left(\prod_{n\ge0}E_n,\ \bigotimes_{n\ge0}\mathcal E_n\right) $$ whose finite-prefix laws are the prescribed iterated integrals $$ \mu_0(dx_0)K_0(x_0,dx_1)K_1(x_0,x_1,dx_2)\cdots K_{r-1}(x_0,\ldots,x_{r-1},dx_r). $$
In particular, if every $E_n=E$ and
$K_n(x_0,\ldots,x_n,A)=K(x_n,A)$, the coordinate process is a homogeneous
$K$-chain with initial law $\mu_0$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Input finite nonempty state and action sets, upper reward estimates $\widetilde r(s,a)$, empirical transition laws $\widehat P(\cdot\mid s,a)$, nonnegative transition radii $b_p(s,a)$, a tolerance $\varepsilon>0$, and fixed orders of the states and actions for tie-breaking. For a vector $v\in\mathbb R^S$, write $\operatorname{span}(v)=\max_s v(s)-\min_s v(s)$ and let $\Delta(S)$ be the probability simplex on $S$. Initialize $u_0(s)=0$. At iteration $i\ge1$, compute
$$u_i(s)=\max_{a\in A(s)}\left[\widetilde r(s,a)+\max_{q\in\Delta(S):\|q-\widehat P(\cdot\mid s,a)\|_1\le b_p(s,a)}q\cdot u_{i-1}\right].$$
For every state-action pair $(s,a)$, run the following transfer routine using $v=u_{i-1}$. Put $q=\widehat P(\cdot\mid s,a)$, $c=\min\{1,b_p(s,a)/2\}$, and order the states $x_1,\ldots,x_m$ by nondecreasing $v(x_j)$, using the fixed state order to break ties. Set $j=1$ and $\ell=m$. While $c>0$ and $j<\ell$, advance $j$ while $q(x_j)=0$, then decrease $\ell$ while $j<\ell$ and $q(x_\ell)=1$. If $j\ge\ell$, stop. If $v(x_j)\ge v(x_\ell)$, stop. Otherwise set $d=\min\{c,q(x_j),1-q(x_\ell)\}$, replace $q(x_j)$ by $q(x_j)-d$ and $q(x_\ell)$ by $q(x_\ell)+d$, and replace $c$ by $c-d$; repeat. Call the resulting vector $q_{i,s,a}$.

For each state, compute $B_i(s,a)=\widetilde r(s,a)+q_{i,s,a}\cdot u_{i-1}$ for every action, record the first action $a_i(s)$ in the fixed action order attaining $\max_{a\in A(s)}B_i(s,a)$, and set $q_i(\cdot\mid s)=q_{i,s,a_i(s)}$. If $\operatorname{span}(u_i-u_{i-1})<\varepsilon$, return the stationary deterministic policy $\pi_i(s)=a_i(s)$, its corresponding transition rows $q_i$, the vector $u_{i-1}$ used in that backup, and the iteration index. Otherwise continue. The procedure is partial unless a separate termination result applies.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the policy path laws used in the expectations below. For a finite MDP with bounded rewards, a policy assigns a probability distribution on $A(s)$ to each finite observed history ending in state $s$, with each action probability a measurable function of the history; deterministic policies are included. For states $x,y$, start at $S_0=x$ and define $\tau_y=\inf\{t\ge0:S_t=y\}$, with $\tau_y=+\infty$ if $y$ is never hit. This is an extended nonnegative measurable random variable because $\{\tau_y\le n\}=\bigcup_{t=0}^n\{S_t=y\}$. Take the expectation and the infimum over policies in $[0,+\infty]$. The MDP is communicating if $\inf_\pi\mathbb E_x^\pi[\tau_y]<\infty$ for every ordered pair $(x,y)$. Its raw diameter is $D_0=\sup_{x,y}\inf_\pi\mathbb E_x^\pi[\tau_y]$ in $[0,+\infty]$, and its normalized diameter is $D=\max\{1,D_0\}$ in the extended order. Since $S$ is finite, $D_0$ is finite for every communicating MDP. Thus a one-state MDP has $D_0=0$ and $D=1$.

derivations.claim: For a probability vector $p$ and $0\le\alpha\le1$, the ball $Q=\{q\in\Delta(S):\|q-p\|_1\le2\alpha\}$ equals the set of $z+w$ with $0\le z\le p$, $\sum z=1-\alpha$, $w\ge0$, and $\sum w=\alpha$. If $q\in Q$, the coordinatewise minimum $p\wedge q$ has mass $1-\|p-q\|_1/2\ge1-\alpha$; scaling it down to mass $1-\alpha$ gives $z\le q$, and $w=q-z$. This also covers $\alpha=0$; for $\alpha=1$, take $z=0$. Conversely, $p-z$ and $w$ are nonnegative vectors of mass $\alpha$, so $\|z+w-p\|_1\le2\alpha$. Thus the support function is $\alpha\max_jv(j)+H_p^\alpha(v)$, where $H_p^\alpha(v)=\max_{0\le z\le p,\,\sum z=1-\alpha}z\cdot v$. The maximizing sets are nonempty and compact, since the simplex and the coordinatewise constrained sets are closed and bounded. The formula includes radii at least $2$, for which $\alpha=1$ and the ball is the whole simplex.

Fix a center $p$, a value vector $v$, and $\alpha=\min\{1,b/2\}$. Each routine update preserves the coordinate sum, keeps coordinates in $[0,1]$, and transfers at most the remaining budget $c$. Since every transfer has $j<\ell$ and the pointers move only inward, its source and destination supports remain disjoint; the final vector is a probability vector at distance $2R\le2\alpha\le b$ from $p$, where $R$ is the total transferred mass. Any feasible $q'$ moves a mass $R=\|q'-p\|_1/2\le\alpha$ from coordinates it decreases to coordinates it increases; the decrease capacities are $p_i$ and the increase capacities are $1-p_i$. Its gain $v\cdot(q'-p)$ is at most the gain obtained by removing mass $R$ from the lowest-valued available coordinates and adding mass $R$ to the highest-valued available coordinates. This follows by exchanging any removed mass at a higher-valued source with available mass at a lower-valued source, and any added mass at a lower-valued destination with available capacity at a higher-valued destination. As $R$ increases, the marginal source values are nondecreasing and the marginal destination values are nonincreasing, so the maximum gain increases while the largest remaining destination-minus-source value is positive and cannot increase after that value becomes nonpositive. The routine implements exactly these allocations and stops only when the budget is spent or every remaining marginal gain is nonpositive. Hence it attains the maximum gain over all $R\le\alpha$. Each positive transfer exhausts one of at most $|S|$ source capacities or $|S|$ destination capacities, or spends the remaining budget, so there are at most $2|S|+1$ positive transfers.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability

derivations.claim: Set $V_0(s)=0$ for every state. Backward induction over the finite horizon gives the Bellman recurrence $$V_{n+1}(s)=\max_{a\in A(s)}\left[r(s,a)+\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)V_n(s')\right].$$ For the induction step, suppose that from every state the $n$-step supremum is attained by a deterministic Markov policy and equals $V_n$. Any history-dependent $(n+1)$-step policy may randomize its first action and may condition later actions on the first reward as well as the next state. Conditional on a first action $a$ and one-step outcome $(s',\rho)$, its continuation has expected reward at most $V_n(s')$ by the induction hypothesis, which is independent of the earlier history and reward. Thus its total expected reward is at most $r(s,a)+\sum_{s'}P(s'\mid s,a)V_n(s')$, averaged over its first-action distribution, and this average is at most the displayed maximum. A maximizing action exists because $A(s)$ is finite; choosing it and then using an attaining $n$-step policy from each possible next state attains equality. The base case $V_0=0$ is attained by the empty policy. This proves both the recurrence and that history dependence cannot improve $V_n$; the joint reward/next-state law is handled by its mean reward and next-state marginal. For any $0\le j\le n$, splitting an $n$-step policy into its first $n-j$ and last $j$ rewards gives $V_n(y)\le V_{n-j}(y)+j$: the first part is at most the optimal $(n-j)$-step value and the last part is at most $j$ because rewards lie in $[0,1]$. For any $x,y$ and $\varepsilon>0$, [F2] gives a policy from $x$ whose hitting time $\tau_y$ has expectation at most $D_0+\varepsilon$. Follow it until $y$ is hit, then use an optimal policy for the remaining $n-\tau_y$ steps if $\tau_y\le n$. On $\{\tau_y=j\}$ for each $0\le j\le n$, the conditional expected total reward given the history through time $j$ is at least $V_{n-j}(y)\ge V_n(y)-j$, since pre-hit rewards are nonnegative. On $\tau_y>n$, the total reward is nonnegative and $V_n(y)\le n<\tau_y$. Summing over the hitting-time events and taking expectations using [F5]–[F8] gives $V_n(x)\ge V_n(y)-\mathbb E[\tau_y]\ge V_n(y)-D_0-\varepsilon$. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ and interchanging $x,y$ proves $\max_s V_n(s)-\min_s V_n(s)\le D_0$.

Put $a_n=\max_s V_n(s)$; the maximum exists because $S$ is finite, and $0\le a_n\le n$ by [F1,F8]. For any $(m+n)$-step policy from $s$, the expected first $m$ rewards are at most $V_m(s)$, while conditional on the complete history through state $S_m$ the remaining $n$-step rule is an admissible policy from $S_m$ and its conditional expected reward is at most $V_n(S_m)\le a_n$. By [F4,F5,F6,F7], the unconditional expected total is therefore at most $V_m(s)+a_n\le a_m+a_n$, so $a_{m+n}\le a_m+a_n$. Conversely, choose $s_*$ attaining $a_m$ and use an optimal $m$-step policy from it; after observing $S_m=z$, continue with an optimal $n$-step policy from $z$. By step 1.1, $V_n(z)\ge a_n-D_0$ for every $z$, so [F4,F6,F7] give total expected reward at least $a_m+a_n-D_0$. Hence $a_{m+n}\ge a_m+a_n-D_0$, and $|a_{m+n}-a_m-a_n|\le D_0$.

Apply [F3] to $(a_n)$ with $C=D_0$ to obtain $a_n/n\to\rho^*$ for some finite $\rho^*$. Step 1.1 gives $a_n-D_0\le V_n(s)\le a_n$ for every $s$, so division by $n$ proves $V_n(s)/n\to\rho^*$ for every state. The bounds $0\le V_n(s)\le n$ imply $\rho^*\in[0,1]$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the interaction path law. The learner is given a finite nonempty state set $\mathcal S$, a finite nonempty action set $A(s)$ for each $s\in\mathcal S$, the observed initial state $s_1\in\mathcal S$, a horizon $T\ge1$, a confidence parameter $\delta\in(0,1)$, and fixed orders of the states and each state's actions. Let $S=|\mathcal S|$ and $A=\max_{s\in\mathcal S}|A(s)|$. Its unknown environment is a finite communicating MDP on $\mathcal S$ and these action sets with rewards in $[0,1]$; the transition kernel, reward laws, and their means are not inputs to the learner. At interaction $t$, the learner observes the current state $S_t$, chooses an admissible action, and then observes the realized reward $\rho_t$ and next state $S_{t+1}$.

Initialize $t=1$ and $S_1=s_1$. At the start $t_k$ of episode $k$, let $N_k(s,a)$ be the total number of visits to $(s,a)$ before $t_k$. If $N_k(s,a)>0$, let $\widehat r_k(s,a)$ be the mean of the rewards observed on those visits and $\widehat P_k(\cdot\mid s,a)$ their empirical next-state law. If $N_k(s,a)=0$, set $\widehat r_k(s,a)=0$ and set $\widehat P_k(\cdot\mid s,a)$ to the point mass at the first state in the fixed state order. Put $n_k(s,a)=\max\{1,N_k(s,a)\}$ and
$$b^r_k(s,a)=\sqrt{\frac{7\log(2SAt_k/\delta)}{2n_k(s,a)}},\qquad b^p_k(s,a)=\sqrt{\frac{14S\log(2At_k/\delta)}{n_k(s,a)}}.$$
Set $\widetilde r_k(s,a)=\min\{1,\widehat r_k(s,a)+b^r_k(s,a)\}$. Run extended value iteration with these estimates/radii and tolerance $1/\sqrt{t_k}$, obtaining a stationary deterministic policy $\pi_k$. Set every within-episode count $v_k(s,a)=0$ and execute the following loop. While $t\le T$, observe $S_t$, choose $a_t=\pi_k(S_t)$, observe $\rho_t$ and $S_{t+1}$, increment $v_k(S_t,a_t)$ and the all-history count for $(S_t,a_t)$, record this reward/transition observation, and retain the observed next state as the current state for the next interaction. Increment $t$ by one. End the episode immediately after an interaction when its pair's count reaches $v_k(s,a)=\max\{1,N_k(s,a)\}$, where $N_k$ remains the episode-start count; if $t\le T$, begin the next episode, otherwise terminate. All action and transition-vector ties use the fixed orders.

Input finite nonempty state and action sets, upper reward estimates $\widetilde r(s,a)$, empirical transition laws $\widehat P(\cdot\mid s,a)$, nonnegative transition radii $b_p(s,a)$, a tolerance $\varepsilon>0$, and fixed orders of the states and actions for tie-breaking. For a vector $v\in\mathbb R^S$, write $\operatorname{span}(v)=\max_s v(s)-\min_s v(s)$ and let $\Delta(S)$ be the probability simplex on $S$. Initialize $u_0(s)=0$. At iteration $i\ge1$, compute
$$u_i(s)=\max_{a\in A(s)}\left[\widetilde r(s,a)+\max_{q\in\Delta(S):\|q-\widehat P(\cdot\mid s,a)\|_1\le b_p(s,a)}q\cdot u_{i-1}\right].$$
For every state-action pair $(s,a)$, run the following transfer routine using $v=u_{i-1}$. Put $q=\widehat P(\cdot\mid s,a)$, $c=\min\{1,b_p(s,a)/2\}$, and order the states $x_1,\ldots,x_m$ by nondecreasing $v(x_j)$, using the fixed state order to break ties. Set $j=1$ and $\ell=m$. While $c>0$ and $j<\ell$, advance $j$ while $q(x_j)=0$, then decrease $\ell$ while $j<\ell$ and $q(x_\ell)=1$. If $j\ge\ell$, stop. If $v(x_j)\ge v(x_\ell)$, stop. Otherwise set $d=\min\{c,q(x_j),1-q(x_\ell)\}$, replace $q(x_j)$ by $q(x_j)-d$ and $q(x_\ell)$ by $q(x_\ell)+d$, and replace $c$ by $c-d$; repeat. Call the resulting vector $q_{i,s,a}$.

For each state, compute $B_i(s,a)=\widetilde r(s,a)+q_{i,s,a}\cdot u_{i-1}$ for every action, record the first action $a_i(s)$ in the fixed action order attaining $\max_{a\in A(s)}B_i(s,a)$, and set $q_i(\cdot\mid s)=q_{i,s,a_i(s)}$. If $\operatorname{span}(u_i-u_{i-1})<\varepsilon$, return the stationary deterministic policy $\pi_i(s)=a_i(s)$, its corresponding transition rows $q_i$, the vector $u_{i-1}$ used in that backup, and the iteration index. Otherwise continue. The procedure is partial unless a separate termination result applies.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the path laws in the concluding UCRL2 application. For any finite nonempty state/action system, probability-vector empirical centers, finite nonnegative transition radii, and real value vector, the transfer routine in extended value iteration returns a feasible vector maximizing the value-vector expectation over the stated $\ell^1$ confidence set; it uses at most $2|S|+1$ positive transfers per row. If the upper rewards are finite, the tolerance is $\varepsilon>0$, and every transition radius is strictly positive, extended value iteration terminates. With fixed state and action orders, its returned policy, transition rows, value vector, and stopping index are measurable functions of the real input estimates. More precisely, write $F$ for its optimistic Bellman operator, put $\eta=\min_{s,a}\min\{1,b_p(s,a)/2\}>0$, and set $u_0=0$, $u_i=F(u_{i-1})$. Then
$$\operatorname{span}(u_i-u_{i-1})\le(1-\eta)^{i-1}\operatorname{span}(u_1),\qquad i\ge1.$$
When $\eta=1$, the span is zero for $i\ge2$. In particular, the positive UCRL2 confidence radii give finite stopping with tolerance $1/\sqrt{t_k}$ in every episode of a finite communicating MDP, including episodes whose confidence set misses the true model.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the policy path laws used in the expectations below. For a finite MDP with bounded rewards, a policy assigns a probability distribution on $A(s)$ to each finite observed history ending in state $s$, with each action probability a measurable function of the history; deterministic policies are included. For states $x,y$, start at $S_0=x$ and define $\tau_y=\inf\{t\ge0:S_t=y\}$, with $\tau_y=+\infty$ if $y$ is never hit. This is an extended nonnegative measurable random variable because $\{\tau_y\le n\}=\bigcup_{t=0}^n\{S_t=y\}$. Take the expectation and the infimum over policies in $[0,+\infty]$. The MDP is communicating if $\inf_\pi\mathbb E_x^\pi[\tau_y]<\infty$ for every ordered pair $(x,y)$. Its raw diameter is $D_0=\sup_{x,y}\inf_\pi\mathbb E_x^\pi[\tau_y]$ in $[0,+\infty]$, and its normalized diameter is $D=\max\{1,D_0\}$ in the extended order. Since $S$ is finite, $D_0$ is finite for every communicating MDP. Thus a one-state MDP has $D_0=0$ and $D=1$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the path laws and conditional-expectation constructions used by the common-average-reward result. For a finite communicating MDP, let $\rho^*$ denote the common optimal average reward. The existence and independence of this value from the initial state are proved in the immediately cited theorem. Assume the Axiom of Choice for the path-space construction. Fix a finite-horizon interaction of length $T$ in a finite MDP with bounded rewards and any nonanticipating policy: each action distribution is a measurable function of the revealed history, and policy randomization is independent of unexposed MDP samples. Assume AC. Let $(M_k,\mathcal F_k)_{k=0}^n$ be a martingale. Suppose finite $\mathcal F_{k-1}$-measurable $A_k,B_k$ and deterministic $c_k\ge0$ satisfy
$$A_k\le M_k-M_{k-1}\le B_k,\qquad B_k-A_k\le c_k$$
almost surely. Then for every $t>0$,
$$\mathbb P(M_n-M_0\ge t)\le \exp\!\left(-\frac{2t^2}{\sum_{k=1}^n c_k^2}\right),$$
and the analogous lower-tail bound holds, with the zero-denominator expression interpreted as $0$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Fix $T\ge2$. At any integer time $t\ge1$, use [F4] to apply [F5] to every fixed pair and prefix length $1\le n<t$. Rewards give two-sided probability $2e^{-2nu^2}$; subset indicators give the same bound. For probability vectors $p,q$, $\|p-q\|_1=2\max_{B\subseteq S}|p(B)-q(B)|$, by summing positive coordinates of $p-q$. Union over $2^S$ subsets therefore bounds an $\ell^1$ error exceeding $u$ by $2^{S+1}e^{-nu^2/2}$. Substituting the algorithm's radii, and unioning over at most $SAt$ pairs and prefixes, bounds reward failure at time $t$ by $2SAt(\delta/(2SAt))^7\le\delta/(64t^6)$, and transition failure by $SAt2^{S+1}(\delta/(2At))^{7S}\le\delta/(32t^6)$. The latter follows from $S2^{1-6S}\le1/32$, whose value at $S=1$ is $1/32$ and whose successive ratio is $(S+1)/(64S)<1$. Unobserved-pair reward radii exceed $1$ and transition radii exceed $2$, so their defaults cannot fail. Since $\sum_{t\ge1}t^{-6}\le1+\int_1^\infty x^{-6}dx=6/5$, with probability at least $1-\delta/8$ every confidence set at every time contains the true transition/reward means. Denote this event by $E$. There is no conditioning on an adaptively selected count in this argument.

In an episode whose confidence set contains the true model, let $F$ be its optimistic Bellman operator. Its iterates $U_n=F^n0$ are optimal $n$-step values for the extended transition choices and fixed upper rewards, by finite-horizon backward induction and attained maxima. Upper rewards are in $[0,1]$, and true transitions and rewards are dominated admissible choices. Thus $U_n\ge V_n$. Also $\operatorname{span}(U_n)\le D$: from $x$, follow a true-model policy hitting $y$ in expected time at most $D+\xi$, and then an optimal remaining-horizon extended policy. The inequality $U_n(y)\le U_{n-j}(y)+j$ follows by dropping the last $j$ rewards, each at most one. For hitting time $\tau$, this yields total expected reward at least $U_n(y)-\mathbb E\tau$, including $\tau>n$ because $U_n(y)\le n$ and rewards are nonnegative. Take $\xi\downarrow0$ and interchange $x,y$. A true history policy's state/action path law can be realized in the extended system by its conditional action probabilities given state/action history; finite histories have finite state/action alphabets, so this averaging preserves its state transitions and hitting-time law.

Let $h_k$ be the vector used in the terminating backup, and let $d_k=F(h_k)-h_k$, with extrema $m_k,M_k$. By [F2], $M_k-m_k<\varepsilon_k=1/\sqrt{t_k}$. Monotonicity and additive homogeneity give $F^nh_k\le h_k+nM_k\mathbf1$. Also $F$ is sup-norm nonexpansive, since $v\le w+c\mathbf1$ implies $Fv\le Fw+c\mathbf1$ and conversely. Therefore $U_n\le h_k+nM_k\mathbf1+\|h_k\|_\infty\mathbf1$. Combine with $U_n\ge V_n$ and [F3], divide by $n$, and pass to the limit to get $\rho^*\le M_k$. Consequently $d_k(s)\ge\rho^*-\varepsilon_k$. For the chosen action and row, $d_k(s)=\widetilde r_k(s,a)+q_k(\cdot\mid s,a)h_k-h_k(s)$. On a good episode, $\widetilde r_k-r\le2b^r_k$ and $\|q_k-P\|_1\le2b^p_k$; step 2.1 gives $\operatorname{span}(h_k)\le D$. Centering $h_k$ halfway between its extrema bounds its sup norm by $D/2$, so $(q_k-P)h_k\le Db^p_k$. Hence each step of that episode obeys $\rho^*-r(s,a)\le (Ph_k)(s,a)-h_k(s)+Db^p_k(s,a)+2b^r_k(s,a)+\varepsilon_k$.

Subtract $\min h_k$ from each episode vector. On good episodes it lies in $[0,D]$. For the probabilistic argument define $w_k$ to be that vector when the episode's confidence set contains the true means and zero otherwise. This is measurable at the episode start, since true means are fixed parameters; its coordinates always lie in $[0,D]$. The increments $X_t=(Pw_{k(t)})(S_t,A_t)-w_{k(t)}(S_{t+1})$ are conditionally centered with conditional range width at most $D$. The reward differences $Y_t=r(S_t,A_t)-\rho_t$ are conditionally centered with width at most $1$, even if reward and next state are correlated. Apply [F5] separately with failure probability $\delta/4$ to obtain $\sum_{t\le T}X_t\le D\sqrt{(T/2)\log(4/\delta)}$ and $\sum_{t\le T}Y_t\le\sqrt{(T/2)\log(4/\delta)}$. These events and $E$ jointly have probability at least $1-\delta$, by step 1.1 and a union bound. On their intersection every episode is good; the sum of $(Ph_k)(S_t,A_t)-h_k(S_t)$ equals $\sum X_t$ plus episode endpoint differences, each at most $D$.

Write $K=\sum_s|A(s)|\le SA$ and $Q_T=\sum_{k,s,a}v_k(s,a)/\sqrt{\max\{1,N_k(s,a)\}}$. By the stop rule in [F1], every within-episode count satisfies $0\le v_k(s,a)\le\max\{1,N_k(s,a)\}$; when $N_k(s,a)>0$ and that pair triggers the episode, its total count changes from $N_k(s,a)$ to $2N_k(s,a)$. For a fixed visited pair, the first observation contributes one. Thereafter, for $N\ge1$ and $0\le v\le N$, rationalization gives $v/\sqrt N=(\sqrt{N+v}-\sqrt N)(\sqrt{1+v/N}+1)\le(1+\sqrt2)(\sqrt{N+v}-\sqrt N)$. Telescoping, including the first observation, and then Cauchy--Schwarz yield $Q_T\le(1+\sqrt2)\sum_{s,a}\sqrt{N_T(s,a)}\le(1+\sqrt2)\sqrt{SAT}$. A completed episode can be charged to a triggering pair. A pair with final count $N$ receives at most $1+\log_2\max\{1,N\}$ charges, because after its initial observation every charge doubles its total. The last incomplete episode adds at most one. Thus concavity of $\log$ gives $m\le1+K+K\log_2(1+T/K)$. When $T\ge K$, this is at most $K(3+\log_2(T/K))\le4\sqrt{KT}\le4\sqrt{SAT}$. For the last inequality set $x=T/K\ge1$: $4\sqrt x-3-\log_2x$ is positive at $1$ and has derivative $(2\sqrt x-1/\log2)/x>0$, since $\log2>1/2$.

On the joint event of step 4.1, sum step 3.1 and use $\max\{1,N_k(s,a)\}\le t_k\le T$. Suppose $S=1$. Then $D=1$ by [F3], every Bellman vector $h_k$ has a single coordinate, and both transition rows are the point mass at the only state. Hence $(Ph_k)(S_t,A_t)-h_k(S_t)=0$ and $(q_k-P)h_k=0$ identically. The episode endpoint differences and the transition martingale increments $X_t$ in step 4.1 are also zero. For every measurable $g:E\to\mathbb R$ with $0\le g\le M$ pointwise, one also has

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space

$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and

On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Write $\operatorname{kl}(p,q)$ for Bernoulli relative entropy. For $0<p<p+e<1$, $$\operatorname{kl}(p,p+e)=\int_p^{p+e}\frac{x-p}{x(1-x)}\,dx\le\frac{e^2}{2p(1-p-e)}.$$ Indeed, differentiating $p\log(p/x)+(1-p)\log((1-p)/(1-x))$ gives the integrand, and $x(1-x)\ge p(1-p-e)$ on the integration interval. Suppose two environments differ only at a single state-action pair $j$, at which one Bernoulli observation parameter changes from $p$ to $p+e$. Let $P_0$ and $P_j$ be their complete histories through the $T$th transition/reward, and let $N_j$ count uses of pair $j$. Their likelihood ratio is the product of the changed Bernoulli likelihood ratios at those uses. The initial law and all conditional action kernels are identical and cancel, including for randomized algorithms. Taking logarithms, conditioning on each past history and selected action, and summing gives exactly $$\operatorname{KL}(P_0\Vert P_j)=\mathbb E_0[N_j]\operatorname{kl}(p,p+e).$$ There is no absolute-continuity issue because both Bernoulli parameters lie strictly between zero and one and every unchanged kernel has the same support. The displayed identity also follows directly by expanding the finite history probabilities; all rewards used below have finite support. Since $0\le N_j\le T$, Pinsker implies $$\mathbb E_jN_j\le\mathbb E_0N_j+T\sqrt{\operatorname{KL}(P_0\Vert P_j)/2}.$$ For a family of $K$ candidate pairs with $n_j=\mathbb E_0N_j$ and $\sum_j n_j\le mT$, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $K^{-1}\sum_j\sqrt{n_j}\le\sqrt{mT/K}$. These arguments hold for every algorithm without a deterministic-policy reduction.

If $S$ is odd, include one additional bare routing state. Arrange the bad states and the optional bare state into a breadth-first rooted $b$-ary tree of height $h$. At each bad state, $B$ useful actions have reward zero and move to its good partner with probability $p$, otherwise staying put. The remaining $b+1$ actions route deterministically toward the parent or one of the $b$ child slots, with missing slots giving self-loops; their rewards are zero. At each good state all $A$ actions have reward one and move to the paired bad state with probability $p$, otherwise staying put. At the optional bare state use the same routing actions and duplicate them to obtain exactly $A$ actions, all with reward zero. This uses exactly $S$ states and exactly $A$ actions per state. For each of the $K$ useful pairs $j$, environment $M_j$ changes just that pair's probability of entering its good state from $p$ to $p+e$. The baseline $M_0$ has no change. Fix the initial state at the bad root. Every environment is communicating.

For every integer $A\ge10$, $$B\ge\frac7{12}A,\qquad B\le\frac23 A,\qquad b\ge A^{2/5},\qquad 2b^2\ge A^{6/5}.$$ For the first inequality, $A\ge12$ gives $B\ge2A/3-1\ge7A/12$, and $A=10,11$ are immediate. The second follows from $\lfloor A/3\rfloor\ge(A-2)/3$. For the last inequality, check $A=10,11,12,13$ directly; for $A\ge14$, $b\ge A/4$ and $A^{4/5}\ge8$, so $2b^2\ge A^2/8\ge A^{6/5}$. This last inequality implies $b\ge A^{2/5}$ because $A^{1/5}\ge\sqrt2$. The number of tree vertices is $n=\lceil S/2\rceil$. If $h=2$, breadth-first filling implies $n\ge b+2$, so $S\ge2b+3\ge2A/3\ge A^{4/5}$ and hence $h\le(5/2)\log_A S$. citations.quote: Let $S$ be a finite nonempty state set and let $A(s)$ be a finite nonempty action set for each $s\in S$, as in the finite-MDP convention. Put $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$ with its discrete sigma-algebra. Equip $S$ with its power-set sigma-algebra, $[0,1]$ with its Borel sigma-algebra, and $S\times[0,1]$ with the product sigma-algebra. A finite MDP with bounded real rewards specifies a probability kernel $Q$ from $D$ to $S\times[0,1]$; equivalently, each admissible $(s,a)$ has a probability measure $Q(\cdot\mid s,a)$ on that product measurable space. The reward-coordinate projection $(s',\rho)\mapsto\rho$ is measurable because the preimage of each Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$ is the product rectangle $S\times B$. Define the next-state law by $P(s'\mid s,a)=Q(\{s'\}\times[0,1]\mid s,a)$ and the mean reward by $r(s,a)=\int_{S\times[0,1]}\rho\,Q(ds',d\rho\mid s,a)\in[0,1]$. At each time, conditional on the observed history and the selected action, the next-state/reward pair has this law. Assume the Axiom of Choice for the path-space construction under policies.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the policy path laws used in the expectations below. For a finite MDP with bounded rewards, a policy assigns a probability distribution on $A(s)$ to each finite observed history ending in state $s$, with each action probability a measurable function of the history; deterministic policies are included. For states $x,y$, start at $S_0=x$ and define $\tau_y=\inf\{t\ge0:S_t=y\}$, with $\tau_y=+\infty$ if $y$ is never hit. This is an extended nonnegative measurable random variable because $\{\tau_y\le n\}=\bigcup_{t=0}^n\{S_t=y\}$. Take the expectation and the infimum over policies in $[0,+\infty]$. The MDP is communicating if $\inf_\pi\mathbb E_x^\pi[\tau_y]<\infty$ for every ordered pair $(x,y)$. Its raw diameter is $D_0=\sup_{x,y}\inf_\pi\mathbb E_x^\pi[\tau_y]$ in $[0,+\infty]$, and its normalized diameter is $D=\max\{1,D_0\}$ in the extended order. Since $S$ is finite, $D_0$ is finite for every communicating MDP. Thus a one-state MDP has $D_0=0$ and $D=1$.
